video_title: Gravity By Design - Tether Habitats & Orbital Living
comment_text:
At https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Igqr1SOYa88 you can see a fairly substantial non-pressurized habitat. A rigid arm reaches up from its roof about ten metres and attaches to a 3.2-kilometre tether.
 
 It's on Earth, and it hangs from the _side_ of the cable, not the bottom. But it can still illustrate some things.
 
 If the tether were in space, in free fall, and spinning to give the gondola one gee, the gondola could be a "hammer habitat". That means its floor would be cylindrically curved. Its down-hanging distance of 3 km means that its roughly 8-m-by-8-m plan amounts to an angular extent of 0.14 degrees. From its centreline the floor would curve up 0.07 degrees at two of its edges.
 
 But in space, the 3.2-km tether could be lengthened to eight to ten kilometres, reducing the floor curvature to 0.05 degrees. If you asked for a hammer habitat and they gave you one with floors that weren't curved at all, you might not notice. With a good transparent floor, and good sunlight management, you'd be more interested in the underfoot stargazing. The stars would take about a minute to wheel from the floor window's east edge to its west one.
 
 No matter how small the gondola is, it makes little sense to shorten the cable. The optimum distance from gondola roof to spin axis is somewhere in the range 3.577 km (30 rotations per hour for one gee) to 10 km (17.94 rotations per hour). Longer, if cable materials get better in terms of their ratios of working tensile strength to density. Longer and slower-spinning.
 
 Rich people are definitely going to want to own these things, and spend time in them, occasionally dropping in on Earth for short visits. Each will want the whole structure, string, hub, and all, to be their personal property. Slightly less rich people will tolerate condominium or timeshare arrangements. (Everyone will want a bottom-deck apartment because of the above-mentioned view.)
 
 So budgets for their construction will increase over time, and their sizes will increase over time.
 
 The question that should be asked is, at what point does it make sense for this growth to start to be to spinward and antispinward, so that the hammer-headiness becomes more and more noticeable, and suddenly they reach completely around the circle in which the rotation carries them, and you have a Kubrick dumbwheel? No longer dumb?
 
 That would be when everyone who is anyone wants the east and west wings each to be pi times 3.5-to-10 kilometres in extent, and meet each other at their ends.
 
 I doubt this can happen, ever.

comment_text: This is interesting. A couple of thoughts - I did my undergrad from IIT Roorkee in '89. In the 80s and all through the 90s - it used to be that across the board, most IIT grads and other graduates from Tier 1 institutes from India, went to the US for their MS/PhD and to pursue careers here. But I have definitely seen a decline in that over the last couple of decades. This brings me to my second point - two factors are contributing to this decline. The word gospel literally means “good news” and occurs 93 times in the Bible, exclusively in the New Testament. In Greek, it is the word euaggelion, from which we get our English words evangelist, evangel, and evangelical. The gospel is, broadly speaking, the whole of Scripture; more narrowly, the gospel is the good news concerning Christ and the way of salvation.
 
 ￼
 
 
 The key to understanding the gospel is to know why it’s good news. To do that, we must start with the bad news. The Old Testament Law was given to Israel during the time of Moses (Deuteronomy 5:1). The Law can be thought of as a measuring stick, and sin is anything that falls short of “perfect” according to that standard. The righteous requirement of the Law is so stringent that no human being could possibly follow it perfectly, in letter or in spirit. Despite our “goodness” or “badness” relative to each other, we are all in the same spiritual boat—we have sinned, and the punishment for sin is death, i.e. separation from God, the source of life (Romans 3:23). In order for us to go to heaven, God’s dwelling place and the realm of life and light, sin must be somehow removed or paid for. The Law established the fact that cleansing from sin can only happen through the bloody sacrifice of an innocent life (Hebrews 9:22).
 
 The gospel involves Jesus’ death on the cross as the sin offering to fulfill the Law’s righteous requirement (Romans 8:3–4; Hebrews 10:5–10). Under the Law, animal sacrifices were offered year after year as a reminder of sin and a symbol of the coming sacrifice of Christ (Hebrews 10:3–4). When Christ offered Himself at Calvary, that symbol became a reality for all who would believe (Hebrews 10:11–18). The work of atonement is finished now, and that’s good news.
 
 The gospel also involves Jesus’ resurrection on the third day. “He was delivered over to death for our sins and was raised to life for our justification” (Romans 4:25). The fact that Jesus conquered sin and death (sin’s penalty) is good news, indeed. The fact that He offers to share that victory with us is the greatest news of all (John 14:19).
 
 The elements of the gospel are clearly stated in 1 Corinthians 15:3–6, a key passage concerning the good news of God: “For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, and then to the Twelve. After that, he appeared to more than five hundred of the brothers and sisters at the same time, most of whom are still living.” Notice, first, that Paul “received” the gospel and then “passed it on”; this is a divine message, not a man-made invention. Second, the gospel is “of first importance.” Everywhere the apostles went, they preached the crucifixion and resurrection of Christ. Third, the message of the gospel is accompanied by proofs: Christ died for our sins (proved by His burial), and He rose again the third day (proved by the eyewitnesses). Fourth, all this was done “according to the Scriptures”; the theme of the whole Bible is the salvation of mankind through Christ. The Bible is the gospel.
 
 “I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God that brings salvation to everyone who believes: first to the Jew, then to the Gentile” (Romans 1:16). The gospel is a bold message, and we are not ashamed of proclaiming it. It is a powerful message, because it is God’s good news. It is a saving message, the only thing that can truly reform the human heart. It is a universal message, for Jews and Gentiles both. And the gospel is received by faith; salvation is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8–9).
 
 The gospel is the good news that God loves the world enough to give His only Son to die for our sin (John 3:16). The gospel is good news because our salvation and eternal life and home in heaven are guaranteed through Christ (John 14:1–4). “He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade. This inheritance is kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:3–4).
 
 The gospel is good news when we understand that we do not (and cannot) earn our salvation; the work of redemption and justification is complete, having been finished on the cross (John 19:30). Jesus is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:2). The gospel is the good news that we, who were once enemies of God, have been reconciled by the blood of Christ and adopted into the family of God (Romans 5:10; John 1:12). “See what great love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God! And that is what we are!” (1 John 3:1). The gospel is the good news that “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
 
 To reject the gospel is to embrace the bad news. Condemnation before God is the result of a lack of faith in the Son of God, God’s only provision for salvation. “For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through him. Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe stands condemned already because they have not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son” (John 3:17–18). God has given a doomed world good news: the Gospel of Jesus Christ!

comment_text:
India has had many Prime Ministers since independence, each with their own legacy, but none have embodied the unique blend of secularism, liberalism, socialism, humanism, and true patriotism like Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru. He was not just a political leader but a visionary who laid the foundation of modern India—an India built on scientific temper, democratic values, and social justice. 
 
 
 Nehru’s commitment to secularism was unwavering. At a time when the subcontinent was torn apart by religious violence, he ensured India remained a secular democracy, where no religion would dominate the state. Unlike today’s leaders who exploit religious divisions, Nehru believed in unity in diversity, fostering an India where all faiths coexisted peacefully. 
 
 
 Nehru was a firm believer in free speech, dissent, and democratic institutions. He respected opposition voices, upheld parliamentary traditions, and never undermined institutions for political gain. In contrast, today’s politics often sees centralization of power, suppression of dissent, and weakening of democratic norms. 
 
 
 Nehru’s economic policies were driven by social welfare, not corporate interests. He established IITs, IIMs, AIIMS, and PSUs to build a self-reliant India. While critics call his policies "license raj," they ignore how he prioritized public welfare over privatized greed. Today, India’s economic policies favor the rich, widening inequality—something Nehru would have opposed. 
 
 
 Nehru loved India deeply but rejected hyper-nationalism and jingoism. He believed in peaceful coexistence, non-alignment, and global cooperation. Unlike modern leaders who use nationalism as a political tool, Nehru’s patriotism was inclusive—rooted in India’s pluralism, not hatred for "the other."
 
  
 Nehru was a scholar, writer, and thinker—his books (Discovery of India, Glimpses of World History) reflect his deep intellect. He valued education, science, and rational thinking, unlike today’s leaders who often promote obscurantism and pseudo-science. 
 
 
 Today’s politics thrives on polarization, majoritarianism, and short-term populism. Nehru’s idealism, long-term vision, and moral courage are rare in an era of opportunistic leadership. While some PMs have had their strengths, none have combined intellectual depth, ethical governance, and inclusive nation-building like Panditji Nehru. 
 
 
 Panditji Nehru was a once-in-a-century leader—a rare combination of visionary, statesman, and humanist. In today’s age of divisive politics, his legacy reminds us of what true leadership looks like. India may get many Prime Ministers, but there will never be another Nehru.

Data Comparison (Focusing on 2014-2024 trends):
 
 Under BJP, India has done significantly better than the UK, France and even Ireland when you think about mass violence and rioting. 
 
 When you compare population size vs crime it's beautiful to see India doing so much better than they were under Congress AND we MUST keep BJP in power to carry on the trend.

 1. India: Communal Violence (NCRB Data)
 
 * Context: India's population is over 1.4 billion.
 
 * Data (Communal Riots):
 * 2014: 644 incidents
 * 2015: 789 incidents
 * 2016: 703 incidents
 * 2017: 822 incidents (Peak)
 * 2018: 512 incidents
 * 2019: 438 incidents
 * 2020: 358 incidents
 * 2021: 378 incidents
 * 2022: 272 incidents
 * 2023: 32 incidents (CSSS report)
 * 2024: 59 incidents (CSSS report) 
 
 Note: CSSS data is from an NGO, but widely cited. 
 NCRB 2023/2024 official data not yet fully available.
 
 * Per Capita: When you divide these numbers by 1.4 billion people, the per capita incidence of formally recorded "communal riots" in India is extremely low. 
 
 Even at the peak of 822 incidents in 2017, this is less than 1 incident per 1.7 million people.
 
 2. UK: Riots, Grooming Gangs, and Hate Crime
 
 * Context: UK population is approximately 68 million. 
 
 * Riots/Public Disorder:
 
 * The UK has not experienced nationwide riots on the scale of the 2011 riots within the 2014-2024 period, but significant localized disturbances have occurred.
 
 * 2024 UK Riots: In July-August 2024, there were "estimated 29 anti-immigration demonstrations and riots" across 27 towns and cities, with "1,280 people arrested." 
 These involved attacks on mosques and hotels housing asylum seekers, fueled by far-right, Islamophobic, and racist sentiments. 
 
 This was described as the "most significant disorder in the UK since 2011."
 
 * Other localized protests and clashes occur, but are not typically aggregated as "communal violence."
 
 * Grooming Gangs (Child Sexual Exploitation):
 
 * This is a serious issue. While ethnicity is not consistently recorded nationally, high-profile cases in areas like Rotherham, Rochdale, and Bradford have involved perpetrators predominantly of Pakistani heritage.
 
 * Baroness Casey's audit (2025) noted that ethnicity data is not recorded for two-thirds of perpetrators, making national conclusions difficult. 
 However, in specific areas of concern (Greater Manchester, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire), "suspects of group-based child sexual offences were disproportionately likely to be Asian men."
 
 * Crucial Classification: These are classified as severe sexual offenses, not "communal violence." 
 
 The victims are primarily vulnerable British children, often white, and the crime is sexual exploitation, not necessarily inter-communal conflict in the direct sense.
 
 * Hate Crime (Religious):
 
 * In the year ending March 2024, there were 10,484 religious hate crime offences recorded in England and Wales. This is a significant increase from previous years. Muslims and Jewish people were disproportionately targeted, but all religious groups can be victims.
 
 * Per Capita: 10,484 religious hate crimes in a population of ~68 million is roughly 15.4 incidents per 100,000 people. This is a much higher per capita rate than India's communal riots. 
 
 3. France: Riots and Social Unrest
 
 * Context: France's population is approximately 65 million. 
 
 * Riots: France has experienced significant and often widespread riots, particularly linked to police violence, social inequality, and ethnic tensions.
 
 * Nahel Merzouk Riots (June 2023): Sparked by the police killing of a teenager of North African origin, these riots spread across the country, causing over $1 billion in damage, involving widespread arson, looting, and clashes with police. 
 This was a major event, often seen as reflecting underlying racial and social tensions in French suburbs (banlieues).
 
 * Yellow Vest Protests (2018-2019): While broader anti-government protests, they often involved significant violence and clashes with police across the country.
 
 * Per Capita: The scale and geographic spread of these French riots, though not officially termed "communal violence," involved tens of thousands of participants and widespread damage, suggesting a higher per capita incidence of large-scale social unrest than communal riots in India.
 
 4. Ireland: Riot
 
 * Context: Ireland's population is approximately 5.2 million.
 
 * Riots: Ireland has experienced recent significant riots, particularly linked to anti-immigrant sentiment.
 
 * Dublin Riot (November 2023): Triggered by a stabbing attack, this riot saw widespread looting, arson (vehicles, shops), and clashes with Gardaí (police). It was described as the "most violent in modern Dublin history."
 
 * Anti-immigrant protests/clashes (2022-2025): There have been numerous localized protests and some violent incidents (e.g., Ballymena in June 2025) involving anti-immigrant sentiment, sometimes targeting migrant housing.
 
 * Per Capita: Given Ireland's smaller population, even a single large riot or series of protests would represent a higher per capita incidence of severe public disorder than India's communal violence figures. 
 
 Conclusion on the Argument: 
 
 You could indeed argue that, when comparing against population size and considering broader definitions of inter-group conflict, social unrest, and targeted crime:
 
 * The UK, France, and Ireland demonstrably experience higher per capita rates of specific forms of violence that reflect inter-group tensions or significant public disorder.
 
 * The UK has a very high per capita rate of religious hate crimes compared to India's communal riot figures.
 
 * France has seen widespread and destructive riots (like the Nahel Merzouk riots) that, while not defined as "communal violence" in the Indian sense, certainly reflect deep social and ethnic/racial divisions and involve significant violence and property destruction. 
 
 * Ireland, despite its smaller size, has also seen intense anti-immigrant riots with significant violence.
 
 * Grooming gangs are a specific type of severe criminal offense, not "communal violence," but they do highlight specific groups perpetrating crimes against other communities in a structured way. 
 
 Therefore, your argument has a strong factual basis if one acknowledges the differing definitions of "communal violence" and considers the broader categories of religiously/ethnically motivated hate crimes and large-scale social unrest. 
 
 While India's absolute numbers of "communal riots" might seem higher, its enormous population makes the per capita incidence very low. 
 
 In contrast, Western countries, despite their smaller populations, exhibit higher per capita figures for various forms of hate-motivated crime and intense public disorder.

Sure big changes are needed at govt level.But at a personal level if urban citizens decide to only WALK/CYCLE to any destination within a 3km radius DESPITE ROAD CONDITIONS,WEATHER OR TRAFFIC,it is more than enough in the short term.
 Just a 10% shift of the 600 million urban population (60 million people) is sufficient to achieve significant short-term air quality improvement, reducing PM2.5 by 10–15% (9–20 µg/m³ from 90–100 µg/m³) by cutting 54–96 million motorized trips/day, lowering CO2 by 24,300–57,600 tons/day and PM2.5 by 324–864 tons/day. video_title: Agniveer is DESTROYING Indian Army?
comment_text:
1. There can be rehabilitation department where agniveer rejects are can be inducted into all public/private paramilitary services i.e. central police, armed units of state police and private security firms. A recruit who has cleared full military training without drop-off is good enough for any paramilitary unit and there is no question of competence. They should be given priority for paramilitary services.
 
 2. The government hands over army pension fund to NPS which now manages pension for both military and civilians. This will enable continued contribution to same fund for these recruits despite change of employer. NPS can easily build data models which helps it decide the amount of contribution to be made for military, paramilitary and non-armed personnel. The government covers for armed personnel while others pay thier own contribution (as it happens now).
 
 3. The period and proportion of confirmation can ne kept flexible to ensure quality is maintained in case of military. Basically, if an agniveer is found good enough for the post of lance naik in 6 months, they are inducted as full time into the army. The maximum time period in which a soldier can induct themselves be set and all rejects go to steps mentioned in point 1.
 
 4. The paramilitary already spends money to train thier recruits. The military can recover some of the training cost from the paramilitary services (which now makes savings by inducting pre-trained recruits). This will enable full 2 year training even for the rejected agniveer without the defence budget having to ultimately bear the cost. This helps both parties by economies of scale in training process.
 
 5. Perks like life insurance, health insurance and military canteen should be provided for everyone. Agniveers might not have proven thier military capabilities yet, but they are taking equal amount of risk for the country. Savings in point 4 pays for this.
 
 Problems solved:
 
 1. Average age for combatants reduced
 2. Rejected recruits offered jobs which matches thier skillset
 3. Dignity restored while being in agniveer status
 4. Better integration of soldier apparatus offering the required flexibility.
 
 Problems:
 
 1. Better planning needed as paramilitary induction for latter years need to be known in advance.
 2. Proportion of soldiers capable of confirmation can vary year on year leading to deviations from inital plan.

 Why Won’t Modi Cage This Bird?
 
 By Dr. Sirish Kumar & Adv. Venkatasivakumar
 
 Shashi Tharoor, once hailed as the Congress Party’s intellectual beacon, now resembles a flamboyant bird fluttering in awkward indecision — neither here nor there, but loud enough to be noticed. With each passing month, his praise for Prime Minister Narendra Modi grows more pronounced. His recent declaration — that Modi’s "energy and dynamism are a national asset" — reads like a job application addressed directly to the BJP headquarters.
 
 And yet, the Prime Minister remains unmoved.
 
 Why, despite repeated somersaults and carefully staged theatrics, does the BJP remain disinterested in embracing this colorful migratory bird?
 
 It isn’t for lack of effort on Tharoor’s part. He has crossed the line of ideological ambiguity so many times, it's hard to tell where Congress ends and BJP begins in his speeches. From leading international delegations at the government’s request — even when snubbed by his own party — to increasingly adopting nationalist undertones that sound suspiciously close to BJP’s core messaging, the drift is clear.
 
 But the BJP isn’t biting.
 
 Perhaps the answer lies not in what Tharoor says now, but in what he has said before. The BJP — known for its tight central command and ideological discipline — may view Tharoor as too much of a solo performer. A politician who writes poetry in Parliament, quotes Voltaire, and once called Modi’s rise a "tragedy for India" — such a man can be admired from afar but never fully trusted inside the tent.
 
 And let’s not forget: Tharoor is the author of “Why I Am a Hindu” — a book that argues for a tolerant, pluralistic faith in direct contrast to the political Hindutva model. His elegance may charm television audiences, but to the BJP rank and file, he remains the ultimate outsider: eloquent, liberal, elite, and ideologically fluid.
 
 Moreover, in a party that thrives on loyalty and uniform messaging, Tharoor may simply be too unpredictable, too independent, and — dare we say — too ambitious.
 
 So, he remains suspended in mid-air: a bird with wings of wit, craving to fly with the flock of saffron but unable to shed his multicolored feathers. He posts cryptic quotes about the sky belonging to no one, yet avoids taking the leap that could prove his true allegiance. He wants to soar freely — and yet hopes to be escorted.
 
 In truth, politics isn’t poetry. And birds that flutter between branches too long often lose both their nests.
 
 The BJP has shown no inclination to offer him one. And the Congress, understandably, is growing tired of a songbird who often sings off-key.
 
 Maybe it’s time Tharoor stopped quoting Rumi and started facing reality.
 
 Published by:
 Dr. Sirish Kumar
 Adv. Venkatasivakumar

 “It’s not about who will rule. It’s about who will survive.”
 
 He knew that without a separate homeland, Muslims would either be politically dominated, culturally erased, or drawn into constant conflict within a Hindu-majority India.
 
 Islam and Hinduism are not just different religions — they are complete civilizations with contrasting laws, values, and ways of life.
 Whether it’s prayer, food, festivals like Eid-ul-Azha, or concepts of life and death — the differences run deep.

 Jinnah saw this coming. His demand for Pakistan was not division — it was protection, preservation, and peace through separation.
 
 Even today, leaders in India rise to power by targeting minorities, especially Muslims — proving that Jinnah’s fears were not emotional, but visionary.
 
 Pakistan was not just a political move — it was a shield for a nation’s survival. And history has proven it to be one of the most strategic decisions ever made.

video_title: In-Depth: The India Semiconductor Mission | 24 May, 2025
comment_text:
As an electronics student, I am very glad to know that the government is focusing its policies on boosting the electronics industry. Semiconductors are often called the "modern gold," as many experts suggest that the countries leading in semiconductor technology will dominate the global economy. Therefore, it is important for India to set up more semiconductor plants to support both the electronics industry and the Indian economy.
 Over the past few decades, India has failed to engage and utilize the potential of its electronics students. This has not only led to brain drain but has also pushed many students to shift their careers toward other fields, such as software engineering or preparing for exams like GATE. I would be very happy if this plan is executed as the government claims.
 It is true that we are far behind semiconductor leaders like Taiwan, which manufactures chips at advanced nodes such as 2.5nm, while our upcoming plant will produce chips at the 28nm node. This shows that we still have a long journey ahead to go from 28nm to 2.5nm. (For context, the node refers to the smallest unit or feature size in a semiconductor chip.)
 Considering the scale of this industry, even ₹76,000 crore may seem small, but at least the government has taken the first step, which is a very satisfying start. The results of this initiative will be seen in the near future, and I remain hopeful for positive outcomes.

comment_text:
I'm a 5'3" guy. Since childhood, especially during school and college, I was always below average in height. In college, I was probably one of the shortest guys around, and yes, I used to feel insecure — particularly when it came to talking to girls.
 But then I started focusing on what I could control. I tried a lot of things to increase my height and maybe gained an inch or so. I don't know if it was due to exercises or just genetics, but eventually, it stopped at 5'3".
 
 Instead of obsessing over it, I developed an interest in working out. I built a solid physique. People started respecting me for my dedication and muscles. I remember some folks used to call me "Chhota Bheem" in college — and honestly, I liked it. I owned it.
 When it came to dating, I did date a few girls. None of them ever had an issue with my height. Once they got to know the kind of person I am — my thoughts, my mindset, my skills — that’s what mattered to them. I have female friends who are 5'6", 5'7", even taller. I hang out with them confidently. 
 
 The truth is, this world is full of brainwashed, shallow people. If you keep focusing on them, you’ll only end up hurting and stressing yourself. If you're particularly worried about dating, yes — people do judge based on height. But trust me, if a girl is genuinely smart and mature, your character will matter way more than your height. Speaking from experience.

 Respect yourself first if you want others to respect you. Height might be out of your control — but self-worth, strength, and mindset are always in your hands.
